extracted.intended_audience: public relations instructors and communication department faculty designing PR writing courses
extracted.subtask_description: An instructional-model for integrating personal computers/word processing into undergraduate public relations writing courses to increase creativity, flexibility, teamwork, and management skills while preparing students for the job market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: make the computer disappear as a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'make the computer disappear as a machine' — present the computer so it functions like a familiar writing tool rather than an intimidating technical object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies (computer = typewriter/pencil; disk = paper); avoid heavy technical detail up front; present only essential actions so the student's focus remains on writing rather than on the machine. The instructor should remove machine-ness through framing and lab design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: view the computer as another tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the computer as another tool in the writer's toolkit rather than as an end in itself or a programming exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize application to public relations writing tasks (formatting, multiple drafts, versions) rather than teaching computer science. The goal is skillful use for communication tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: use the computer as a management tool to support, enhance, and improve writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computer features to support stages of the writing process (editing, time-limited work, rewrites, multiple copies, version control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: produce multiple copies for peer review, store drafts in directories, meet deadlines with rapid revisions, maintain logs/to-do lists, and use the computer to simulate real-world production workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: enhance creativity in the classroom
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage the computer's capacity for rapid text entry and revision to increase idea generation and creative exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign brainstorming exercises that prioritize flow of ideas (keep fingers moving, don't self-edit), allow multiple versions, and provide instant editing feedback so students can iterate and explore beyond usual stopping points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize using computers as tools, not requiring computer science coursework
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration should focus on tool use for PR students rather than forcing formal computer science classes which may defeat the communication objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide application-oriented instruction; avoid imposing programming or extensive technical prerequisites on liberal-arts PR students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide open computing laboratories staffed with professional consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing assignments beyond class should be completed in open labs where consultants assist students with practical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labs should be accessible for outside-class work, staffed by knowledgeable consultants to troubleshoot hardware/software issues and help students use word processing tools effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize information overload: provide concise, essential instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid heavy manuals and jargon; give short step-by-step guides for basic operations needed for assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide two-page procedures (formatting, opening a document, saving, printing, exiting) and a keyed grid of keyboard functions placed around the typing pad for individual assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor must be comfortable with hardware and software
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor needs hands-on familiarity because student breakdowns will range widely and will require instructor troubleshooting and guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for both mechanical problems (cables, drives) and usage issues; anticipate a range of student skill levels and common failures (e.g., forgetting to save).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with brainstorming exercises on the computer
rubrics_metrics.description: First lab assignment should focus on brainstorming to reduce pressure for polished copy and to foster idea flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word processing to let students type as fast as they think, de-emphasize correctness, have multiple short sessions, and allow instructor to respond to technical breakdowns while preserving creative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide supervised hands-on practice on word processing software
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure each student has at least one supervised session to use the word processor and learn basic options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow brainstorming with a short supervised lab so students can explore keyboard options and software features with instructor/consultant support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce a short news release for peer/instructor review and rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a brief news release assignment to teach producing multiple copies for peer and instructor editing and the rewrite process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing is less onerous when not handwritten; circulate at least three copies for review, return edits for rewriting, and archive the news release in the directory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach management skills through workflow responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should manage production logistics: initial creation, printing, contacting editors, distributing multicopies, deadlines, and assessing development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students maintain weekly 'to do' lists and activity logs that can be shared with teammates; computer tools make tracking and updating goals easier and visible to peers and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require creating multiple versions/formats from a single idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Train students to adapt one message into different formats (e.g., pitch letter, news feature, PSA 10s/30s/60s) by duplicating and editing a single base document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice saves time and cultivates listening/oral phrasing skills when students read PSAs aloud; it also demonstrates format-specific editing and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulate team writing and real-world production conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use team assignments, peer editing, timed deadlines, and distribution to simulate agency/corporate PR workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-supported team tasks encourage collaboration, easier sharing of drafts, and a realistic sense of production demands that agencies expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checker and build a personal 'red-flag dictionary'
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage spell-check features and have students create a custom list of frequently misspelled words to reduce recurring errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some errors reflect typing habits; maintain an individualized red-flag dictionary to catch habitual mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide necessary hardware/software resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should ensure access to appropriate equipment (PCs), software (word processors like Microsoft Word with spell check), disks, and multicopy printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minimal set of resources (multiple stations, disks, printing capability) is required to support the described instructional model effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing students to purchase manuals; offer in-lab support
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not require students to buy software manuals; instead, supply concise help sheets and in-lab assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer optional printed step-sheets and make consultants available so students learn tool use without extra expense or intimidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow practical exceptions for students facing access issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Accommodate commuting students or those affected by technical breakdowns by permitting typewriter completion when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the curriculum emphasizes computers, permit occasional non-computer submission if access problems occur, with the expectation that the course sequence will use computers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize professionalism and marketability gained from computer experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-based coursework should aim to produce professional-quality student work and marketable technical competence attractive to agencies and employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internship reports and employer feedback as evidence; note that students have been hired because of their unique computer experience and produce more professional work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design assignments to increase production under time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computer-supported tasks to enable students to complete more rewrites and assignments within limited time, increasing practice and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because editing and duplication are faster, students can practice more iterations, improving final output and management experience.
